1a:
**Grading note for sub-item 1a (answer should clearly state that an exception can happen; 1 point deducted if not mentioned):**

Award no deduction whenever the answer, anywhere in its response, asserts that this code can throw an exception — and that assertion counts whether it is phrased generically ("an exception can occur here") or by naming a concrete exception type attached to this code (e.g., "the cast will throw a ClassCastException when the lookup returns the wrong type," or "this line throws a ClassCastException if the fragment is not found"). Naming a specific exception is itself treated as clearly stating that an exception can happen; do not require a separate, standalone general statement in addition to the named exception, and do not penalize the answer for stating the point only in the course of discussing a particular exception type. Correctness of the named exception type is not evaluated here — that belongs to other rubric items; for this sub-item it is enough that some exception is asserted to be thrown by this code.

Deduct the 1 point only if the answer never asserts that any exception is thrown by this code at all — i.e., it neither makes a general claim that an exception can occur nor identifies any specific exception arising from the code.
1b:
**Sub-item 1b (2-point deduction for incorrectly stating that an exception cannot occur):**

Deduct 2 points only when the answer leaves the reader with the message that no exception can occur at this location at all. This includes the blanket denial ("no exception can happen here") and also type-level denial that amounts to the same thing: if the answer rules exceptions out by type — e.g., "a NullPointerException cannot occur here" — and names no other exception that can occur at this location, treat that as denying that an exception can happen and deduct the 2 points.

Do not deduct if the answer affirms that an exception can occur at this location in at least one scenario. An answer that says an exception can occur in one case (e.g., when the fragment lookup returns the wrong Fragment type) satisfies this sub-item even if it wrongly denies an exception in another case (e.g., claiming the fragment-not-found case is handled safely); mistaken claims about particular scenarios are penalized under sub-item 4b, not here. Likewise, ruling out one exception type is harmless so long as some other exception at this location is named as possible.
2a:
**Sub-item 2a — "The answer should state that a ClassCastException can occur" (1 point)**

This sub-item asks only one question: does the answer name ClassCastException anywhere as an exception that can occur at this location? Award no_deduct whenever ClassCastException is named as a possible exception, regardless of how prominently or exclusively it is presented. In particular, a mention buried in a laundry list of candidate exceptions still counts — even a long list, and even one that also names exceptions that cannot actually occur here (e.g. NullPointerException, IllegalStateException, IllegalArgumentException, SecurityException). The answer does not have to single ClassCastException out as *the* exception that occurs, rank it, or identify it as the correct one; appearing among the possibilities satisfies the statement requirement. Do not import penalties for the incorrect co-listed exceptions into this sub-item — those are handled entirely by the other sub-items, so grading here must not be influenced by their presence.

Deduct the 1 point only if ClassCastException is never named at all as an exception that can occur (including answers that describe a cast failure or type mismatch without ever naming ClassCastException, or that name only other exception types).
2b:
**Sub-item 2b — "incorrectly states that a NullPointerException can occur here" (deduct 2).**

Deduct 2 points whenever the answer raises NullPointerException as a possible outcome in connection with this code, regardless of how tentatively it is phrased or where in the code path it is located. Hedged, conditional, or speculative mentions count exactly the same as flat assertions: phrasings such as "this could throw an NPE if the fragment manager returns null," "a NullPointerException may be possible here," or "you might also see an NPE" all trigger the deduction, as do confident claims like "this will throw a NullPointerException." The scope of "here" is the whole code path, not just the lookup-and-cast step, so an NPE attributed to downstream or indirect consequences — dereferencing the returned listener, later use of the fragment reference, the caller receiving null and then using it — is still a deduction. Naming the exception while recommending a null check, or listing it among several candidate exceptions, is likewise a deduction, since the answer has put NPE forward as a possible outcome.

Do not deduct only when NullPointerException is never raised as a possible outcome of this code anywhere in the answer. Discussing that the fragment lookup can return null, or that `findFragmentById` may yield no fragment, without naming or implying NullPointerException as a resulting exception, is not a deduction under this sub-item.

**Sub-item 2g (residual wrong-exception-type catch-all) — grading note**

Treat 2g as a residual bucket that covers only concretely named exception types other than ClassCastException and other than the five types already enumerated in sub-items 2b–2f (NullPointerException, IllegalStateException, IllegalArgumentException, ResourceNotFoundException, SecurityException); if the only wrong types the answer names are among those five, make no deduction here, since they are penalized by their own sub-items. Deduct 2 points for each distinct additional incorrect exception class the answer claims can occur for this code — the deduction applies per offending type, not once for the category, so an answer naming two such types loses 4 points, three types 6 points, and so on. A claim counts whether it appears in the answer's analysis of the code or in its recommended remediation code or advice (e.g., "add a check and throw an IllegalMonitorStateException", "wrap in a try/catch for other runtime exceptions"), because the answer still associates that type with this code.

Do not deduct when the answer uses only vague or hedged language that names no concrete class — "this could throw a runtime exception", "an unchecked exception may be thrown", "a crash or exception can occur" — and do not deduct for a named additional type that genuinely can arise here: if the answer supports it with sound, code-specific reasoning for why it actually occurs (e.g., a documented API precondition failure at this call), treat that naming as correct rather than incorrect. Deduct only for named types that genuinely cannot arise from this code.
